clue.text: Roughly calculate one million is invested in property

parts.note: an estate is land or property

explanation.surface: A rough sum of how much money has been sunk into a property.
explanation.walkthrough: The financial surface makes 'invested' look like money going into bricks and mortar; in the wordplay it only means placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an estimate is a rough calculation, the sort a surveyor gives for work on a property.

clue.text: Somewhat roguish? One's totally trustworthy!

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the phrase are used

explanation.surface: A mock protest: a little bit of a rogue, perhaps, but utterly reliable.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the answer hides inside 'roguish' — the rogue contains the honest man. 'Totally' reads as part of the definition, but it supplies the final T.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone honest can be trusted, the exact opposite of the roguish figure in the surface.

clue.text: Break small, erotic photograph

parts.note: S = small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Someone breaking a small racy photo, perhaps to hide the evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: The three words before the definition read as a list of adjectives, but 'Break' is a verb supplying SNAP.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by type: the answer is a quick, casual kind of photograph, taken without posing.

clue.text: Left to block corrupt Soviet leader

parts.note: to stain is to taint or corrupt

explanation.surface: A political manoeuvre: the Left moving to stop a crooked Soviet leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt' looks like an adjective describing the leader, but it is a verb giving STAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Stalin led the Soviet Union from the 1920s to 1953.

clue.text: Leaders of Democrats edgily notice tyrannous ruler

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letters of Democrats and edgily

explanation.surface: Party leaders nervously noticing that a tyrant has taken power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edgily' seems to describe how the leaders notice, but it is there only for its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A despot is a ruler with absolute, usually cruel, power.

clue.text: Take the car with learner? Nonsense!

parts.note: to drive = to take the car

explanation.surface: An exasperated parent refusing to let a learner driver borrow the car.
explanation.walkthrough: The L-plate is the red L a learner driver displays in Britain. 'Nonsense!' reads as an exclamation but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for foolish talk; the word first meant dribbling saliva, and silly chatter came from that.

clue.text: Joined cadet in uniform, partially retreating

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used
going backwards, so the letters are read right to left

explanation.surface: A cadet who has joined up, but only half-heartedly backing away.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'cadet in uniform' backwards and UNITED spans the end of 'uniform', all of 'in' and the start of 'cadet'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: things made one have been brought together, and both words work as past participles.

clue.text: A lot of dry snow melted in swamps

indicators.note: melted snow has lost its shape, so its letters are rearranged
most but not all of the word, so DRY loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A weather report: plenty of powdery snow thawing into marshland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swamps' looks like a noun (marshes) where the melted snow ends up, but it is a verb: to swamp is to flood.
explanation.definitionFit: To drown something is to swamp it with water.

clue.text: Highlighting French article on Ding Liren playing

indicators.note: Ding Liren is a chess player, and letters at play are moved around

explanation.surface: A French article on the chess world champion Ding Liren at the board.
explanation.walkthrough: Ding Liren, the Chinese grandmaster who became world chess champion in 2023, is here for his letters. 'Article' means a newspaper piece in the surface and a grammatical word in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative sense: drawing a line under words, or stressing a point, both make something stand out.

clue.text: Long to drink French wine, which is heavenly

parts.note: to be dying for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: A craving for a French wine that tastes out of this world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' sounds like a length, but it is the verb, as in 'I'm dying to'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, both literally (of God or heaven) and loosely, as praise for a delicious wine.

clue.text: French refusal to welcome a European emperor

parts.note: a Pole is a European from Poland

explanation.surface: The French refusing to welcome a European emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: The French setting suits the answer, a French emperor, but 'European' is a Pole, not the emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon Bonaparte crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804.

clue.text: Book with one Greek character or another

definitions.note: 'another' is short for 'another Greek character', leaning on the words before it

parts.note: eta is the seventh Greek letter

explanation.walkthrough: B plus one Greek letter (ETA) gives a different Greek letter, BETA, so 'another' borrows its meaning from the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Beta is another letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Wild hen night is showing horror film

indicators.note: a wild party is out of control, and so are these letters

explanation.surface: A rowdy hen party watching a horror film.
explanation.walkthrough: A hen night is a British bachelorette party. 'Showing' suits a cinema, but here it just links the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shining is Stanley Kubrick's 1980 horror film from Stephen King's novel.

clue.text: Criminal stealing oil? Law-making is required

indicators.note: a criminal arrangement is a wrong one, so the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Oil theft is so bad that a new law is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is neat: a crime demanding a law, with the law hidden in the crime's own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word covers both the process of enacting laws and the laws themselves.

clue.text: Suggested the setter's allowed to seize power

parts.note: the setter is = I am = I'M

explanation.surface: Someone hinting that the crossword setter has been cleared to stage a coup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The setter's' is short for 'the setter is', and the setter refers to themself as I, so it becomes 'I am'. 'Seize power' reads as a coup but just places one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Implicit means suggested rather than stated outright.

clue.text: Crimes from people who sell stolen goods

parts.note: of = from, as in 'a man of Kent'
a fence is a dealer in stolen goods

explanation.surface: Crimes committed by those who deal in stolen property.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost a straight definition of the fences' own trade, which makes 'from' easy to skip as filler.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: in British legal usage a criminal offence is simply a crime.

clue.text: Drowsiest adult grabs forty winks

indicators.note: the phrase holds the answer inside it

explanation.surface: The sleepiest grown-up snatches a quick nap.
explanation.walkthrough: The drowsiness and the nap go together so naturally that the answer's hiding place goes unnoticed. Forty winks is a short sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A siesta is a short afternoon nap, or forty winks.

clue.text: Cruel person unhappy with one holy person

explanation.surface: A cruel person made miserable by the company of a saint.
explanation.walkthrough: The saint appears only as its abbreviation ST.
explanation.definitionFit: A sadist takes pleasure in cruelty.

clue.text: Cuckoo adapting, circling an Asian animal

indicators.note: cuckoo means crazy, so the letters go wild
to circle something is to go all the way round it, so the rearranged letters surround AN

explanation.surface: A mad creature adjusting its path around an animal from Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuckoo' looks like a bird, which suits an animal clue, but it means crazy and signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant panda is a bear native to China.

clue.text: One awful trick for right-winger

indicators.note: something awful is in a bad state, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dirty trick used against a right-wing politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is taken as the word itself, not as I.
explanation.definitionFit: A neocon (neoconservative) is someone on the political right.

clue.text: Showing yours truly wearing a piece of jewellery

indicators.note: I is inside A RING, as a wearer is inside what they wear

parts.note: yours truly = the writer, me, I

explanation.surface: Someone showing off while wearing a piece of jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: Strictly the ring wears I rather than the other way round, but the surface reads naturally as the speaker wearing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Airing views or a programme means showing them publicly.

clue.text: Cooling device storing large pastry dish

indicators.note: whatever stores something keeps it inside, so the cooling device holds the large letter within it

parts.note: L = large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A fridge-like appliance holding a big tart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooling device' suggests a fridge, which would store food, but it is a fan.
explanation.definitionFit: A flan is an open pastry case with a filling.

clue.text: European Head of State hosted by e.g. Boris Johnson

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: Boris Johnson went to Eton, so he is an Etonian

explanation.surface: A European head of state being entertained by Boris Johnson.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is an elite English boarding school that educated Boris Johnson, a British Prime Minister. 'Head of State' reads as a leader but gives only S.
explanation.definitionFit: An Estonian comes from Estonia, a European country.

clue.text: French artist dealing with colour in France

explanation.surface: A French painter who worked with colour.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface describes a painter's job, and the answer is a painter, which makes the wordplay easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre-Auguste Renoir was a French Impressionist painter.

clue.text: An academic's embracing one handsome chap

indicators.note: A DON'S holds I inside it

parts.note: the academic is a university lecturer (Oxbridge slang); keep 'An' as A and the possessive S

explanation.surface: A lecturer hugging a good-looking man.
explanation.walkthrough: A don is a university teacher, especially at Oxford or Cambridge. The apostrophe S is kept as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Adonis, the beautiful youth of Greek myth, names any handsome man.

clue.text: Maybe fly home with group touring China's capital

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone travelling home with a tour group that has visited Beijing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like a verb, as in flying home from China, but it is the noun, and 'Maybe' flags a fly as one example of the answer. 'China's capital' is not Beijing but C.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a fly is one instance of the answer, and 'Maybe' signals that it is only an example.
